title: Creating More Emphasis Vocally
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This post treats vocal delivery as part of a leader's executive presence. It explains that a slightly higher pitch on key words, at the start or middle of a sentence, signals importance and urgency. The author gives readable exercises, such as stressing absolutely in a sentence about good news, so the reader can hear the effect. He separates rising-falling intonation from uptalk, where pitch climbs at the sentence end and every statement sounds like a question. Uptalk, he warns, undermines a speaker's perceived confidence in professional settings. The takeaway is to raise pitch deliberately on key words so people remember what matters to you.
points: Tone, pitch and vocabulary shape a leader's credibility and executive presence.
A modest pitch rise on a key word conveys emphasis and urgency.
Rising-falling intonation, with a fall right after the rise, is distinct from uptalk.
Uptalk makes declarative sentences sound like questions and erodes perceived confidence.
quotes: Tone, pitch, grammar, and vocabulary combine to establish credibility and to project confidence. The elusive quality of executive presence is, in part, a reflection of vocal style and choices.
Minor variations in pitch can have a dramatic effect on how people interpret what is being said, especially on what is important to the speaker. Words spoken with a higher pitch carry more emphasis.

To test this, say the sentence out loud with your normal pitch and tone. Now, without screeching or creating too much rise, focus on the word absolutely by using a slightly higher pitch. The word now carries emphasis and conveys a very different level of enthusiasm.

This quality is also known as rising-falling intonation because there is always a fall in the pitch immediately following the rise. Don’t confuse this with a continual rise in pitch or pitch that ascends at the end of a sentence. This is known as uptalk and is a speech pattern that conveys a lack of confidence or uncertainty.
In professional settings, uptalk makes every declarative sentence sound like a question, typically undermining the presumed confidence of the speaker.
